title: Link the facts in a reading-buddy composition
instructions: Composition practice. The prompt: ‘Describe a project at your school and explain what it achieved.’ You are writing about a reading-buddy scheme. Your notes: the school library found that first-year students borrowed fewer books than any other year group; to encourage reading, second-year students read with first-year students twice a week for four weeks; 20 first-year students joined; during the four weeks, their average number of reading-log entries rose from two to four a week; of the 20, 14 said reading was more enjoyable, four noticed no difference and two did not answer; the scheme did not measure test scores or whether students kept reading after it ended. Choose the sentences that show how your facts are linked, using only what your notes show. Answer all six questions before viewing feedback.

parts.prompt: Which sentence gives the reason for the scheme most clearly?

options.text: Because first-year students borrowed fewer books than any other year group, the school started a four-week reading-buddy scheme.
First-year students borrowed fewer books than other groups; nevertheless, the school started the scheme for exactly that reason.
After the library checked how many books each year group borrowed, therefore the school started a four-week scheme.
First-year students borrowed fewer books, although the school started the scheme because they enjoyed reading more than before.

choice_rationales.A: The ‘because’ clause gives the recorded reason, and the main clause gives the response.
choice_rationales.B: ‘Nevertheless’ signals a contrast, but the low borrowing was the reason, not a contrast.
choice_rationales.C: ‘After’ already makes the first part a time clause, so adding ‘therefore’ breaks the sentence, and it gives no reason.
choice_rationales.D: ‘Although’ signals a contrast that is not there, and the enjoyment came after the scheme, not before it.

parts.hint: Choose the sentence in which the library's finding explains why the scheme started.
parts.correct_explanation: A clear reason sentence names both the recorded cause and the response it led to.

parts.prompt: Which sentence states what happened next with correct limits and punctuation?

options.text: The scheme started, as a result every first-year student in the school read exactly four books every single week.
The scheme ran for four weeks; during that time, the average number of reading-log entries rose from two to four a week.
Consequently the school has permanently ended every reading problem that its first-year students used to have.
The average number of entries rose from two to four a week, however the scheme had started during those same four weeks of term.

choice_rationales.A: A comma alone joins two clauses, and the claim about every student and four books is not in the notes.
choice_rationales.B: The semicolon is correct, and ‘average’ and ‘during that time’ keep the claim within the notes.
choice_rationales.C: There is no earlier sentence for ‘consequently’ to follow, and the permanent claim goes beyond the notes.
choice_rationales.D: ‘However’ needs a full stop or semicolon before it, and it signals a contrast that is not there.

parts.hint: Keep ‘average’ and the four-week period rather than widening the result.
parts.correct_explanation: A result stays believable when its linking word, punctuation and limits all match the notes.

parts.prompt: Which sentence admits a limit without marking the link twice?

options.text: Although 14 of the 20 students said reading was more enjoyable, but the scheme did not measure test scores.
Despite 14 of the 20 students said reading was more enjoyable, the scheme did not measure test scores.
Although 14 of the 20 students said reading was more enjoyable, the scheme did not measure test scores.
However 14 of the 20 students said reading was more enjoyable because the scheme did not measure test scores.

choice_rationales.A: ‘Although’ and ‘but’ mark the same contrast twice.
choice_rationales.B: ‘Despite’ must be followed by a noun phrase, not a full clause.
choice_rationales.C: One ‘although’ clause is followed by a complete main clause, so the limit is clear.
choice_rationales.D: ‘Because’ makes the missing measurement the reason for the enjoyment, which makes no sense.

parts.hint: Use one contrast word, and check the grammar that follows it.
parts.correct_explanation: ‘Although’ introduces a full clause and does not need an extra ‘but’.

parts.prompt: Which THREE phrases would correctly limit a claim about the scheme?

options.text: during the four-week scheme
among the first-year students who joined
according to the students who answered
for every student in the school from now on
proving that test scores rose for good

choice_rationales.A: It limits the claim to the period that was measured.
choice_rationales.B: It limits the claim to the group that took part.
choice_rationales.C: It limits the enjoyment finding to the students who gave an answer.
choice_rationales.D: No one measured every student or any later period.
choice_rationales.E: The scheme did not measure test scores.

parts.hint: Select limits that the notes really contain: time, group and who answered.
parts.correct_explanation: A useful limit names the exact group, period or source that the evidence covers.

parts.prompt: Which sentence avoids treating ‘it happened afterwards’ as proof of a lasting effect?

options.text: After the scheme started, reading-log entries rose; therefore the scheme turned every first-year student into a keen reader for the rest of their lives.
Reading-log entries rose during the weeks the scheme ran, which suggests it helped, although no one measured whether students kept reading afterwards.
Because entries rose later in the term, the passing of time itself made the first-year students want to read more.
Entries rose after the scheme started, so no other explanation for the change could possibly be true at all.

choice_rationales.A: Order alone does not prove a lasting effect, and no one measured lifelong reading.
choice_rationales.B: It reports the timing, makes a careful claim and states what was not measured.
choice_rationales.C: This invents a cause that the notes do not support.
choice_rationales.D: Order of events alone cannot rule out every other explanation.

parts.hint: Keep what was observed, but limit the claim to what the scheme could show.
parts.correct_explanation: A careful writer can say a result suggests an explanation while stating what was not measured.

parts.prompt: Which paragraph would be the best one to write, with clear and fair links between the facts?

options.text: Firstly, the library checked its records. Moreover, there were second-year students. Furthermore, 14 students answered. In conclusion, the reading-buddy scheme worked and was a great success for the whole school.

Because first-year students borrowed fewer books than any other year group, the school started a four-week reading-buddy scheme. During the scheme, the average number of reading-log entries rose from two to four a week. Although 14 of the 20 students said reading was more enjoyable, four noticed no difference. The results suggest the scheme helped, but it did not measure test scores or later reading.
The school started the scheme, therefore every student read more forever, although but two students did not answer because test scores went up.

After the library checked its records, the average number of entries rose from two to four a week. However, the school started a reading-buddy scheme for four weeks. Despite 14 of the 20 students said reading was more enjoyable, four noticed no difference. Consequently, the scheme proved that test scores rose and that every first-year student kept reading for the rest of the year, both at school and at home.

choice_rationales.A: The linking words are stacked on facts that are not connected, and the conclusion is too strong.
choice_rationales.B: Each linking word shows a real relationship, and the conclusion keeps the scheme's limits.
choice_rationales.C: The links contradict each other, ‘although but’ doubles the contrast, and the claims are not supported.
choice_rationales.D: The order is confused, ‘however’ signals a false contrast, ‘despite’ is followed by a clause and the conclusion goes far beyond the notes.

parts.hint: Choose the paragraph in which every linking word names a real relationship and the conclusion keeps the limits.
parts.correct_explanation: Clear reasoning needs both visible links and fair claims; linking words must serve the evidence, not decorate it.
